units.spoken: Double DQN
Why the highest guess runs high, and the second opinion that fixes it.
A game-playing network's guesses of how well it will do keep climbing far above how well it really does. Why does it run high, and what single change fixes it?

The agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad. Here the agent is a game-playing program. It sees only the screen and its points, never the game's rules.
In its games the state is the screen, a move is a joystick press, and the reward is the change in its points. A good press lifts its points at once; a bad one can end the game many presses later.

An episode is one run from the start until it ends. The games are Atari games, classic home video games played with a joystick. On Atari an episode ends at game over. A game can run for a long time, press after press, before it is over.

Take a look at this figure. The bars are the network's guesses, one score for each press it could make, and the program simply plays the tallest bar. The network never sees the game's rules, only the screen and its points, so those bars are all it has. That is the whole setup: if the bars run high, the program trusts them anyway and plays the tallest one. The question this page answers is what happens when the tallest bar is wrong.

The screen in Figure 1 is a Breakout game, rows of blocks above a paddle and a ball, and each bar is one press's score, a taller bar a higher score. Take a screen where the ball drops low: the tallest bar is the press the program plays next.
Section one, Game-playing networks guess too high

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. On Atari the program cannot see its future points; it has to learn which presses lead to them.

A move's value Q of s and a, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes action a in state s and plays on from there. A Q-table keeps one score for every state and move. A Q-network is a neural network that takes the state and outputs one score per move, in place of the table. After training, the program plays the joystick press whose score is highest.
The discount gamma sets how much a reward one step later still counts. Q-learning's target is the step's reward plus the discounted best score in the next state.

Training a Q-network with Q-learning's target is a Deep Q-Network, DQN for short. DQN pulls each bar toward that target, step after step. Every Atari game ends with a final points total, so the points the program really earns can be counted after play.

On Atari those scores end above the return the learned policy really earns, on some games far above. Double DQN, the method on this page, changes one line of DQN's target to fix this. On Atari, Double DQN's estimates end much closer to the return its policy really earns.

What this figure is teaching is that an estimate and a real return are two different things, and DQN confuses them. DQN's guess about its own play climbs far past the points it really earns, so the program thinks it plays far better than it does. Double DQN's guess settles close to the points its play really earns. When the guess and the real return agree, the scores can be trusted; when they split apart, the program is fooling itself about how well it plays.

In Figure 2, the red line is DQN's estimate, the teal line Double DQN's, and the two dashed lines are the returns the policies really earn, Double DQN's return above and DQN's return below. Take a game late in training: DQN's red line sits far above its dashed line, while the teal line sits on its own dashed line.
Section two, Why the max runs high
The max picks the luckiest guess
Picture one screen where every press is truly worth the same. Each guess still comes out a little off, high here and low there, because the network guesses from the screen alone.
How. The max takes the highest guess, so it picks the press whose error came out highest, not the press that is truly best.
When it works, the scores climb above the points the program really earns, even on a screen where every press is truly worth the same.

Bootstrapping means putting your own current guess for the next state inside the target. On Atari each score's target holds the network's own guess for the next screen, so an error there is copied back.

Overestimation means the values climb above the return the agent really earns, because a max over noisy guesses picks lucky ones. An expected value is the average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is. The sign E marks an expected value.
Equation 1. This card shows the average of that highest guess sits above the worth the presses truly share, and that averaging each press first lands on the shared worth instead.
Take a look at this equation. The average of the highest guess runs high.

The max first line. M is the average of the highest guess. E is the average over the noise, the guess errors. Q hat is the network's guess, scoring a press on this screen. Max picks the highest guess, running over the presses in the screen. Order matters: max first picks the luckiest guess, then the average over the noise. Intuitively, taking the max first lets the luckiest guess win.
Intuition. A max over noisy guesses runs high: the luckiest guess wins, even when every move is truly worth the same.
Example. Take one screen where every press is truly worth the same. Each guess comes out a little off, so one press comes out highest by luck alone.

The average first line. At least means the average of the highest guess is never smaller than the best of the averages. Here the average comes first, so each press's lucky errors cancel, then the max picks the best average. The space between the two sides is the overestimation, the amount the max runs above the true best.
Intuitively, the best of the averages is the true best.
Example. Take the same screen, but average each press over the noise first. The lucky errors cancel, and the best average lands on the shared worth.
So the max first runs high, and averaging first lands on the shared worth.

The dots tell the story. Every dot is one guess for one press, and the guesses spread out on both sides of the worth they truly share, some high and some low, because every guess carries a little error. The ringed dot is the max, the highest guess, and it floats higher than that worth. It is not the true best, it is the luckiest guess. That is why the max runs high even when every move is truly worth the same: the max does not find the best move, it finds the luckiest error.
Figure 3 shows why the max of noisy guesses runs high. Take the ringed dot, the max: it sits above the line, the luckiest guess, not the true best.

The Double DQN paper proves that even fair guesses, right on average, overshoot. More moves make it worse, as the paper's first figure shows. An earlier study showed the overshoot grows with the noise.

sections.section: 3 A second opinion from the target network

units.spoken: Section three, A second opinion from the target network
A second opinion on the pick

Picture two sets of guesses for the same next screen. Double Q-learning trains one set to pick the best-looking move and the other set to score it, so the luck that made a move look best does not also lift its score.
How. Double DQN uses the live network, the one being trained, to pick, and the target network, its slow copy, to score the pick.
When it works, the target sits near the points the program really earns instead of far above them.
In Double Q-learning the roles switch at random from update to update. On Atari, Double DQN needs no new network; it reuses these two.

Follow the next screen through the two networks. It goes to both: the live network picks the best-looking move, and the target network scores that pick, not its own best. That number feeds the target the played move is pulled toward. The two networks see the same screen and give different answers, and that split is the whole fix: the luck that made a move look best does not also lift its score.
In Figure 4 the next screen goes to both networks: the live network picks, and the target network's score for the pick feeds the target.

The target network is a copy of the live one that trails behind it, so it is only partly independent, but its guesses differ enough that a pick's luck lifts its score less. This makes Double DQN a one-line change to DQN that moves it toward Double Q-learning: it changes only the picker and keeps the same network and settings.

The two rows are the whole method in one picture. The top row is the live network, and its highest dot is the pick. The bottom row is the target network, and the dot that counts is the one under the pick, not the bottom row's own highest dot. That lower dot is the score that feeds the target, so the target comes out lower than it would if the target network had picked and scored on its own. The unused highest dot is the luck DQN would have counted and Double DQN leaves out.
Take a screen in Figure 5 where the live row's highest dot sits over a lower dot in the target row: the lower dot is the one used, and the target row's own highest dot is not used.

sections.section: 4 The target splits the pick from the score

units.spoken: Section four, The target splits the pick from the score
One network picks, the other scores

Picture one step the program already played, and the screen it landed on. The target is the number the played move's score is pulled toward, built from the step's points plus the discounted score of the next move.
How. The live network picks the next move with argmax, the move with the largest live score, and the slow copy scores that pick.
When it works, the bars settle near the points the program really earns.
Replay keeps a memory of past steps, and training samples random batches from it. On each remembered Atari step, only the target's next-move choice changes.
A batch is a handful of remembered steps trained on together; the loss averages how far their scores are from their targets.
Equation 2. A game-playing program whose scores keep climbing above the points it really earns needs that one change: a second opinion on the pick.
Take a look at this equation. A second opinion on the pick fixes the climbing scores.

The DQN pick line. A sub D Q N is DQN's pick for the next screen. Q is the slow copy's score for each press on that screen. Phi prime is the target network's weights, the slow copy's. Argmax returns the press itself, not its score, the one with the largest score. The semicolon means Q is computed with the target weights. Intuitively, one network does both jobs, so the pick's luck lifts its score.
Intuition. DQN lets the slow copy both pick the next move and score it.
Example. Take a remembered step landing on a screen where the slow copy scores right highest. DQN picks right and scores it with the same slow copy.

The DQN target line. Y is the target for this remembered step, one number. R is the step's reward, the points just earned. Gamma is the discount, so only that share counts. The score in the target is the slow copy's score for the move it picked. Y equals the reward plus the discount times that score. Intuitively, the target is what the played move's score is pulled toward.
Intuition. The target is the step's reward plus the discounted score of the next move, both from the slow copy.
Example. Take the same remembered step. The target adds the points just earned to the discounted slow-copy score of right.

The live pick line. A sub live is the live network's pick for the next screen. Phi is the live weights, the weights being trained. Argmax again returns the move with the largest score. But the scores now come from the live network. The picker changes and nothing else does: the same screen, the same presses, a different network judging them.
Intuitively, only the picker changes: the live network picks, the slow copy scores.
Example. Take the same next screen. The live network scores fire highest, so fire is the pick, though the slow copy would have picked right.

The Double DQN target line. The score is the slow copy's score for the move the live network picked. Y equals the reward plus the discount times that score. At an episode's last step, the target is only the reward. So the two targets differ in the picker only: the slow copy picks in DQN, the live network picks in Double DQN. Intuitively, the luck counts once, because two networks split the job.
Intuition. The pick and the score now come from different networks, so the luck counts once.
Example. Take the same remembered step. Double DQN's target scores fire, the live network's pick, with the slow copy's score for it.
So DQN's slow copy picks and scores, while Double DQN's live network picks and the slow copy scores.

sections.section: 5 A Double DQN target, step by step

units.spoken: Section five, A Double DQN target, step by step
Here is a remembered step, sampled from memory, whose score moves toward its target.

This figure walks one update through its stages, and the lesson is in the order. The target is built first, from the live network's pick scored by the slow copy, and only then does the bar for the played move move toward it. The bar never moves while the target is still being built, because the bar is pulled toward the target, not the other way round. That order, target first and bar last, is the whole update.

Try stepping through the stages with the Prev and Next buttons. Watch the pick move from the slow copy to the live network at stage three, and watch the target marker appear above the played move's bar before the bar moves at the end.

Figure 6 walks one update through six stages, from the remembered step to the played move's bar moving toward its target. Stage 1 shows the remembered step; stage 2 the live network's row; stage 3 shows the live network picking fire, the tallest bar; stage 4 adds the target network's row, whose tallest bar is right; stage 5 puts the target marker above the played move's bar; stage 6 moves the played move's bar toward the marker. Take the played move's bar: it moves only at the end, once the target is built.

sections.section: 6 The live network picks, the slow copy scores

units.spoken: Section six, The live network picks, the slow copy scores

The target step below comes from the learn step in my Value-based-methods repo on GitHub, the code for one update, with the live network picking and the slow copy scoring. Stable Baselines is a library of reinforcement learning methods. Its DQN has a double_q switch, on by default, that turns this step on.
This code runs one learning step: the live network picks, the target scores.

One. The live network picks the next move, line 3 of the Double DQN card. In argmax(1, keepdim=True), the 1 means pick along the moves, and keepdim=True keeps the pick as one number per screen, the shape gather needs. no_grad tells the code not to record this step for learning, since the target is only read, never trained on.

Two. The target network scores the picked move, and the target is built, line 4 of the Double DQN card. In gather(1, a_live), the 1 means gather along the moves, and a_live is the picked move, so it takes the target network's score for that move. done is 1 on the last step and 0 otherwise, so (1 minus done) is the done mask: it zeroes the next screen's score on the last step, and the target is the reward alone.
For contrast, the DQN target picks and scores with the slow copy alone.
This code is the DQN target for contrast: the slow copy picks and scores.

One. The DQN target for contrast, lines 1 and 2 of the Double DQN card. The slow copy both picks and scores here. max(1, keepdim=True) takes the highest score along the moves, keeping one score per screen.
Section seven, The single max drifting high
The double learner stays near the truth
Picture a small table of move scores in place of a network, so the noise in each guess can be seen. Every move is equally good, yet each guess comes out a little off.
How. The single learner picks and scores with one table, as DQN's target does, and the double learner picks with one table and scores with another.
When it works, the single learner's line on the chart ends above the truth line, the worth the moves truly share, while the double learner's line ends near it.
Before you press Play, try the sliders: with many moves the single curve ends above the truth, and with no noise both curves sit on it.

Look at what the two curves do. The single learner's curve ends above the truth line, because it picks and scores with the same table, so the luckiest guess lifts its own score. The double learner's curve ends near the truth, because one table picks and another scores, so the luck counts once. More moves and more noise push the single curve higher, and the double curve stays put. That split is the whole lesson: one table fools itself, two tables keep each other honest.

Try the sliders first: set many moves and a lot of noise, then press Play. Watch the single curve end above the truth line while the double curve ends near it. Then set no noise and watch both curves sit on the truth.

In Figure 7, dots for the start state's guesses scatter above the dashed truth line, with the single learner's highest guess ringed; below, the red single-max curve ends above the truth line while the teal double curve ends near it.

sections.section: 8 An extra forward pass per learning step

units.spoken: Section eight, An extra forward pass per learning step
Eight point one, The extra pass runs when DQN learns
One extra forward pass
Picture the next screens going through the live network as well as the target network. A forward pass is one run of a network over some screens, giving back one score per move.
How. Double DQN runs the live network over the next screens to pick, then gathers the scores from the target network's outputs.
When it works, the extra run is the only added cost, and the estimates sit close to the points the program really earns.
Eight point two, The settings that differ from DQN

Epsilon-greedy usually makes the move with the highest value and, with a small chance epsilon, a random one instead, so the agent keeps exploring. A soft update moves the target network's weights only a little toward the live network's, with tau as the share moved. The paper reuses the letter tau for the steps between copies. A hard copy overwrites the slow copy with the live weights every so often. The paper's tuned version of Double DQN copied the target less often, explored less and used one shared offset for every move's score.

This table lines up the settings that differ from DQN. The target copy interval is how often the slow copy is refreshed: the tuned version copies every 30,000 frames, three times rarer than DQN's 10,000, while my repo soft-updates instead. Epsilon while learning is the random play during training: the tuned version uses 0.01, a tenth of DQN's 0.1. Epsilon at evaluation is the random play when testing: the tuned version uses 0.001, and my repo does not use it. The output layer is the bias on each move's score: the tuned version shares one bias across moves, while DQN and my repo give each move its own. Everything else is unchanged from DQN. The pattern is less randomness and rarer copies than DQN.
Take the target copy interval row: copying more rarely is the fix.

sections.section: 9 Where the second opinion pays off

units.spoken: Section nine, Where the second opinion pays off

Double DQN fits nearly always wherever DQN fits, because it keeps the same network and changes one line of the target. It pays off most when move scores sit far above returns you can measure, as Figure 2 shows. A normalized score of 0 means random play, and 100 percent means a human expert's play. The paper rates every game this way, so results from different games can be averaged. On Asterix, an Atari game, the paper's score rose from 70 to 180 percent of human play.

sections.section: 10 Where the second opinion falls short

units.spoken: Section ten, Where the second opinion falls short
Keep picker and scorer apart
Picture the two networks drifting together until the pick and the score come from the same guesses. The second opinion only helps while the picker and the scorer are different networks.
Copy the slow copy rarely, so it stays behind the live network, and always take the score from the slow copy, never from the live network.
When it works, the estimates stay near the points the program really earns, and copying more rarely is the first fix when they drift high again.

The learning rate eta sets how big a step each update takes. On Atari, Double DQN adds no setting of its own, so the settings that can break it are the ones it shares with DQN. Divergence means the scores climb without bound instead of settling.

This table lists the ways Double DQN goes wrong and what helps. Copying the target too often makes the picker and the scorer the same network, so overestimation returns; the fix is rarer copies or a smaller soft-update share. If the two sets of guesses are not independent enough, the reduction is smaller than hoped; the fix is a slower target, or full Double Q-learning. Scoring with the live network by mistake gives the same single-network max as plain Q-learning; the fix is to gather from the target network. Instability from other causes, like a learning rate too high or a missing done mask, comes from outside the target; the fix is DQN's fixes. Two independent estimates can lean low, giving slightly pessimistic values; the fix is to accept the slight pessimism. The first two rows are the target drifting too close to the live network, the third is a coding mistake, and the last two are outside the target or a small price worth paying.
Take the target copied too often row: the picker and the scorer become the same network for a while, and the fix copies more rarely or shrinks the soft-update share.
